Product design · Public health

Tracking every vaccine from the national store to a health post with no fridge

VaxTrack is a supply chain app for Nigeria's vaccines. I'm the lead designer on it, so I've worked on both sides: the web dashboard the national and store teams use, and the Android app for the people actually moving the doses.

Client
Federal Ministry of Health, DRIVE Initiative
Role
Lead product designer
Timeline
May 2026 to now
Users
9 roles, web and Android
The problem

Nobody could see where a dose was

Before VaxTrack, moving vaccines from a state store to a clinic ran on handwritten registers and phone calls. Nobody had a live picture of where a dose was, how much was left, or whether the fridge holding it was still working.

So when something went wrong, you heard about it late. Sometimes weeks late. These were the situations the programme team kept bringing up:

Stockouts nobody seesA facility runs out of a vaccine and the state store finds out weeks later.
Deliveries nobody can proveThe driver says the vaccines were delivered. The facility says they never came. Nobody can show either way.
Fridges that fail at nightA fridge stops working overnight and by morning the vaccines are ruined. Nobody was alerted.
Stock in the wrong placeOne facility is holding more than it can use before expiry, and the one down the road has run out.

Every one of those ends the same way, with a child who comes for a vaccine and doesn't get it.

Getting started

I didn't understand the system yet, so I wrote it down first

I won't pretend I walked in knowing how vaccines move around Nigeria. I studied anatomy, so I knew what a vaccine does. I did not know what an LCS was, or why there's a little square on every vial that changes colour.

The team wanted screens quickly, and I understood why. But I didn't want to design for a system I couldn't explain to someone else. So before doing any proper design work, I wrote a PRD in plain English: who uses it, how vaccines move between levels, what each person needs to see first, and the rules every screen has to follow. When I was asked for a timeline on one of our review calls, I said it plainly:

I'm still trying to understand the system on my own to inform my design, so that I don't design what isn't necessary.

Those rules ended up holding the whole product together. They're programme rules, so I don't get to design around them. A store should never hold more than 125% of what it uses in a month. At 50% it's time to reorder. Under 25% it's urgent. At zero it's a stockout and national needs to know straight away. And whatever expires first goes out first. Every stock number in VaxTrack, on the web or on a phone, gets its colour from those lines.

Who it's for

Nine people, four levels, two very different apps

Vaccines move down from national to state to LGA to the facility, and requests move up. Every screen in VaxTrack belongs to someone at one point in that chain.

NationalNational officerSLWG memberWeb
StateState store officerWeb
LGALGA store officerWeb
On the road3PL driverMCCOConveyorAndroid
FacilityEHF in-chargeUHF in-chargeAndroid

The people at the top sit at a desk with a laptop and want to see everything at once, so they get the web dashboard. The five at the bottom are on the road or at a health centre, usually on a budget Android, sometimes outside in the sun with bad network. They get the mobile app, and that's where most of the hard decisions were.

What changed

My first PRD missed a whole person

I was quite proud of that first PRD. Then the programme team read it.

I'd assumed health posts without a fridge would request vaccines in the app like every other facility. That's not how it works at all. No fridge means there's nothing to store. The in-charge tells a conveyor what they need for that day's session, the conveyor collects it in the morning from the equipped facility nearby, drops it off, and takes back whatever wasn't used before the day ends.

That conveyor wasn't anywhere in my document. By the time I was writing the user guide a month later, they had their own app, and a few other things had moved too:

PRD, JuneUser guide, July
Users8 types9, with the conveyor
Health post with no fridgeRequests vaccines in the appTells the conveyor in person, confirms when they arrive
Signing for a deliverySignature on screenA one-time code given to the MCCO
Logging inCode sent by SMSUsername and password from a supervisor

I'm glad I found out on paper. Finding out after building the screens would have hurt a lot more.

The field app

Designing for someone standing outside a clinic in the sun

Picture the driver at a stop. They're parked outside a health centre in the afternoon, the sun is right on the screen, they've got a cooler box in one hand and a cheap Android in the other, and the network keeps dropping.

That picture decided a lot. The main action on every screen is one big button at the bottom where a thumb can reach it, and it says exactly what happens next, like Start trip or I have arrived. Numbers are large and monospaced, because in bright light a 17 can pass for a 71, and that mistake is 54 doses nobody can account for. Every status has a word on it as well as a colour, since colours wash out in the sun. And nothing gets lost when the signal goes. Whatever they've typed stays on the phone and sends when the network comes back.

This is one delivery, followed through everyone who touches it.

3PL driverCarries the vaccines

The driver's day starts with the trip: how many stops, how many doses, and which facility is first. The manifest lists every batch with the closest expiry date on top, because first expiry, first out is a rule and I didn't want the driver to have to remember it. When they tap I have arrived, the facility is told the delivery is outside.

Then they wait while the MCCO counts. Instead of standing there asking if they're done, the driver's screen shows the verification happening, then MCCO verified.

MCCOChecks the vaccines

The MCCO is the government's person on every trip. The driver carries, the MCCO checks. One of them can't close a delivery without the other, and that rule came straight from the programme. It's the only way to settle the argument where one side says the vaccines were delivered and the other says they never came.

The count is where I spent the most time. If the numbers don't match, I didn't want to throw the MCCO into a separate error flow while everyone stands around. The shortfall shows right on the card, Short 33, they type why, and they carry on. The delivery still closes and the gap stays on record for the store to follow up.

EHF in-chargeRuns a facility with a fridge

An equipped facility has its own fridge, so it actually holds stock. The in-charge isn't placing routine orders. They receive deliveries, log what they used after each session and hand vaccines to the conveyor. So their home screen opens on what's running out, worst first.

The part I like most is the code. When the in-charge receives a delivery or hands vaccines to a conveyor, the app gives them a one-time code to show the other person. Until it's typed into the other phone, nothing has moved. It's a small thing, but it means every handoff has two people on it.

ConveyorThe last mile

This is the person who wasn't in my PRD. They go from the equipped facility to a health post, deliver for one session, and bring back what wasn't used, all in the same day.

I designed their flow as one session with two legs, out and back. The return part stays locked until they've submitted what they collected, because you can't return vaccines that never went out. The app also works out diluents and syringes on its own and checks that numbers match full vials, so nobody is doing maths by the roadside.

UHF in-charge, and everyoneThe health post, plus shared screens

The health post has the simplest app in the whole system, on purpose. No fridge means no stock to manage, so they see what's coming and answer one question: did it arrive?

Login, alerts, reporting a problem and the profile work the same way for all five field roles, so the app feels familiar whichever role you're in.

The web dashboard

The dashboard is the opposite problem

The field app is about doing one thing at a time. The national officer needs the opposite. They're looking after 1,759 facilities and want to know what's wrong today.

So the dashboard opens on the eight numbers the programme measures itself by, each one next to its target with a plain label: on target, attention or critical. Under that is every vaccine in every state, and a red cell means zero doses. Click a state and it opens into LGAs, then wards, then facilities, so you can follow a red cell all the way down to the clinic that ran out.

Allocating vaccines to states, tracking deliveries and handling alerts all happen here too. When you create an allocation, it shows what the national store has now and what it'll have after, so nobody gives out stock that isn't there. Alerts open into a side panel with what happened and what to do next.

Setting it up

The call where we fixed the foundation

Some of the most useful design work on this project happened on calls. In a June review the developers showed us a mess. State and LGA names were coming in from different CSV files with different spellings, so the same LGA showed up twice in a dropdown, once in capitals and once without.

We agreed nobody would type the name of a state or LGA again. Those names live in one place, Organisation Units, and everything else pulls from there. When a state uploads its facilities or its microplan, it downloads a template with the names already filled in and locked, adds its own numbers and uploads it back. One of the leads summed it up on the call:

This organisational unit is the main setup of this entire system.

It also means that if VaxTrack ever goes to another country, you change the hierarchy, districts instead of LGAs, and the screens stay the same.

Iterations

None of this is the first version

The Figma file has an archive page full of things I designed and then changed. Some of them I still like. These are the changes that taught me the most.

The national dashboard

My first dashboard tried to show everything that was on fire: a red banner of critical alerts across the top, a grid of states coloured by how they were doing, and a live feed of alerts. It looked busy in a way that felt important. But it answered what's on fire, and the national officer also needs to know how the programme is doing overall. The current one starts with the programme's own numbers against target, then the stock grid, and alerts got a page of their own.

Allocations

The first table had a column for every vaccine, so one allocation stretched right across the screen and you had to scroll sideways to read it. Now each row is one vaccine going to one state, with the action it needs right there on the row.

Receiving a delivery

This one changed the most. In the first version, the facility in-charge counted every vial again on their own phone, checked each vial monitor against a safe and unsafe picture, then signed on the screen. But the MCCO had just counted the same box at the same handover. Now they count it once, together, and the in-charge confirms by giving the MCCO a code. Fewer steps for the person who's least used to apps, and the record is just as strong.

When something goes wrong at a stop

Problems used to have their own screens: a flag issue form, and a separate screen for marking a stop unavailable. Most problems at a stop are a short count, though, so that now happens right on the count card. Anything else goes through one report a problem screen that every role shares.

When a fridge fails

The PRD says a fridge alert can't be just another item in a list, because once the cold chain breaks, those vaccines are gone. For the state store, I made the alert take over the top of the dashboard: the reading, the safe range, how far over it is and how many doses are at risk.

What's next

I want to go out on a delivery

Honestly, that's the thing I want most. Everything in the field app was designed for sun, one hand and bad network, but I designed it remotely on a laptop. I want to stand next to a driver and an MCCO at a real stop and see where it still slows them down.

Writing the PRD first felt slow at the time. Looking back, it's why everything after it moved as fast as it did. And the conveyor taught me that the person most likely to be missing from a requirements doc is the one doing the carrying.
